title: Autopsy and Will
premise: Noor Galloway, a night-shift taxi dispatcher in the rain-soaked city of Verrow, spent years making himself invisible after testifying—under a changed name—as a child witness in a murder trial. When a confession letter arrives for a dead man, postmarked the day after his funeral, Noor realizes the writer knows both the old case and Noor's buried identity. The letter's author, it turns out, is the taxi company's beloved owner, Marguerite Voss, who has been using her fleet to stage deaths that mirror the decades-old crime, forcing Noor to relive it. As Noor secretly reroutes and records her drivers, he discovers she intends the final 'recreation' to end with his own staged suicide—closing the loop on the only witness who could have convicted her brother years ago. Noor traps her by feeding her a falsified route log, broadcasting her final confession to every cab on the night shift, and survives—but only by finally choosing to be seen, testifying again under his real name.
about_author: Rosalind Sterling is the pen name of a former municipal court clerk who spent eleven years transcribing testimony before turning to fiction. She lives in a coastal city she refuses to name, and writes exclusively at night.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Address
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Working the graveyard dispatch shift, Noor routes cabs through Verrow's gray hours and keeps his head down. A letter arrives addressed to a man whose funeral was yesterday. The emotional beat: uneasy curiosity, the itch of something wrong that Noor almost throws away.

chapters.title: Postmarked Tomorrow
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The letter is a detailed confession to a murder Noor recognizes from a case file he should never have seen—the trial he testified in as a child, under another name. The postmark date unsettles him: the day after the funeral. Beat: dread blooming under routine.

chapters.title: Invisibility as a Skill
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, with a flashback. We learn Noor changed his name, his city, his whole texture of life after testifying at nine years old. He built a career on knowing everyone's location while being located by no one. Beat: the fragile architecture of a hidden life.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. A second confession arrives, describing a death that hasn't happened yet—and quoting a detail from Noor's sealed testimony. Someone has the old case file. Beat: the hunter realizes he was always the quarry.

chapters.title: Dispatch Log, Annotated
chapters.summary: Noor pulls the company's route logs and finds a driver's runs match the confession's geography with uncanny precision. His supervisor, Denny, dismisses it as coincidence. Beat: paranoia sharpening into method—Noor starts his own quiet investigation.

chapters.title: Mrs. Voss Remembers Everyone
chapters.summary: Marguerite Voss's POV. The taxi company's owner, warm and formidable, interviews a new driver. She knows every employee's birthday, troubles, debts. Her kindness reads as genuine—until the last line, where she checks a file on Noor Galloway. Beat: charming menace.

chapters.title: The Body on Halden Street
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. A man dies exactly as the second letter predicted. Police call it an accident; Noor recognizes the staging from the old trial's evidence photos. Beat: horror confirmed—the letters are a rehearsal schedule.

chapters.title: Detective Okafor's Cold File
chapters.summary: Detective Adaeze Okafor's POV. Okafor, who worked the original case as a rookie, is quietly haunted by its loose ends. She reopens the file and finds pages missing—pages only someone with institutional access could remove. Beat: a second hunter enters the wood.

chapters.title: What the Child Saw
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, deep flashback. The full memory: nine-year-old Noor watching the original murder through a stairwell, the trial, the acquittal of Marguerite's brother, and the protective custody that erased him. Beat: grief for the self he surrendered to survive.

chapters.title: Routes and Rituals
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He maps Voss's fleet against every death in the confession and finds a pattern: each killing recreates a moment from the old crime, in order, like stations of a cross. Two remain. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of a countdown.

chapters.title: The Driver Who Talked
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor interviews a Voss driver who hints at 'special runs'—unlogged fares, sealed envelopes—then recants and disappears from his apartment. Beat: the cost of knowing, and Okafor's suspicion turning toward the taxi company itself.

chapters.title: A Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Digging through archived payroll ledgers, Noor finds his own birth name in a decades-old expense entry—hush money paid to his family. Voss's company has owned his secret since before he could drive. Beat: violation; the past was never past.

chapters.title: Dinner at the Voss House
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Voss invites Noor to dinner, all warmth and reminiscence, probing his memory of the old neighborhood with surgical delicacy. Noor plays dumb and leaves shaken, certain she knows exactly who he is. Beat: a duel conducted over dessert.

chapters.title: Okafor Comes to Dispatch
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor canvasses the taxi company and interviews Noor, who lies badly about the letters. She leaves him a card and a warning: the next person to die will be someone connected to the original witness. Beat: two secrets circling, nearly touching.

chapters.title: The Penultimate Letter
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The fourth confession arrives, describing the murder of Okafor, dated three days out. Noor must choose: stay invisible and let her die, or expose himself to save her. Beat: the theme made flesh—survival versus complicity.

chapters.title: Breaking Cover
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor meets Okafor at dawn, gives her his real name and the letters, and lays out the pattern. She believes him—but going official means Voss's people inside the department will know within hours. Beat: terror and relief braided together; the weight lifts and the danger doubles.

chapters.title: The Trap Is Set
chapters.summary: Noor and Okafor's alternating POV. They feed Voss a falsified dispatch log showing Noor alone on a remote night route—the final station of her recreation. Okafor's team waits in the dark. Beat: coiled tension; the hunted turns hunter.

chapters.title: Halden Street, Again
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The trap springs wrong—Voss anticipated the police, sent a decoy, and takes Noor herself at cab-point, revealing the last 'recreation' was always his staged suicide, closing the case forever. Beat: the floor drops out; survival now means wit, not backup.

chapters.title: The Confession Broadcast
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Held in a cab on an open channel, Noor goads Voss into reciting her brother's crime and her decades of staged deaths—every word live to every radio on the night shift, Okafor listening, drivers recording. Beat: the climax; voice as weapon.

chapters.title: Arrest on the Empty Route
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Cabs converge from every direction, boxing Voss's car in a sea of headlights. Okafor makes the arrest while dispatchers—Noor's invisible army—hold the perimeter. Beat: triumph of the overlooked; the night shift saves its own.

chapters.title: Testimony, Second Time
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In a courtroom, Noor testifies under his real name, voice steady, the child in the stairwell finally allowed to speak. Voss is convicted. Beat: catharsis; identity reclaimed at the price of the invisibility that once kept him alive.

chapters.title: Night Shift, After
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Weeks later, Noor returns to dispatch—not hiding now, just working. A new dispatcher asks how he survived it all. He answers honestly. The phones ring; the city goes on. Beat: quiet resolution; survival was never free, but it was worth its price.
